## v0.1 — v0.1

`··········` 0% · 0 of 20 done · due 2026-10-31

`oath run hello.oath` runs a pure program. `oath swear hello.oath` checks every keeper against its oath's examples, records the verdict in a store keyed by the oath's hash, and prints it. Every call site resolves through the oath to a sworn keeper. Editing an oath un-swears its keepers, visibly. That last line is the idea, and it is in v0.1 so a stranger feels it on day one.

## v0.2 — v0.2

`··········` 0% · 0 of 20 done · due 2027-01-10

Oaths carry `law` properties checked by small-scope enumeration with the smallest counterexample. State lives in effect cells; every write is journaled, so `try` rolls back correctly without anyone writing an inverse. External ops declare a compensation; irreversible ops are refused where rollback is promised. Effectful keepers can be sworn because the world is rewound after each example, and `given`/`then` let examples and laws speak about state. `oath trace` steps backwards through the journal.

## v0.3 — v0.3

`··········` 0% · 0 of 12 done · due 2027-02-13

A hole is an oath with no keeper, and now reaching one at runtime fires the `Keep` effect instead of failing. Three keeper sources ship: pause into a REPL, search the store for a keeper of an equivalent oath, and pipe the oath to an external command and swear whatever comes back in a sandbox. When keepers from different sources disagree, the differential check says where.

## v0.4 — v0.4

`··········` 0% · 0 of 12 done · due 2027-04-10

Programs span files. `use ./lib.oath` imports by path; `use sort = oath:<hash>` imports one promise by its hash and never mentions its name. Renaming an oath breaks no importer. An imported oath with no sworn keeper is a hole, and `Keep` fires for it like any other. `oath ls` browses the store.

## v1.0 — v1.0

`··········` 0% · 0 of 12 done · due 2027-06-30
